content: Boza is a widely consumed fermented beverage in countries such as Albania, Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Romania, Serbia, and Turkey. In Turkey, it is traditionally made from fermented wheat, while in Bulgaria and Romania, it is prepared using wheat or millet. The drink is characterized by its thick consistency, low alcohol content (approximately 1%), and a mildly acidic, sweet flavor. In North Macedonia, boza is notably thinner, lighter, and sweeter in taste. In Turkey, it is customarily served with cinnamon and roasted chickpeas, primarily during the winter months. Historically, the Ottoman Empire provided boza to its army due to its high carbohydrate and vitamin content. In Bulgaria, it is a staple of the traditional breakfast pairing of Banitsa with Boza. In Albania, boza is predominantly produced and sold in the northern regions, with availability in candy and ice cream shops in the capital, Tirana. In southern Serbia, boza is produced and distributed throughout the country. The Romanian variant, known as bragă, is sweeter than the Turkish and Bulgarian versions but thicker and darker than the Macedonian type. The origins of boza trace back to ancient Anatolian and Mesopotamian populations. The Ottomans adopted and disseminated the recipe across their empire. The Greek historian Xenophon documented the production of boza in eastern Anatolia as early as 401 BC, noting its storage in clay jars buried underground. The drink remained localized until the Turks popularized it under the name boza, derived from the Persian word buze, meaning millet. Boza reached its peak popularity during the Ottoman era, becoming a prominent trade in urban centers. Until the 16th century, boza was widely consumed, but the introduction of a variant containing opium, known as Tartar boza, led to its prohibition by Sultan Selim II (1566–1574). Despite these restrictions, the Turkish traveler Evliya Çelebi noted that boza remained popular, with 300 shops employing over 1,000 people in Istanbul alone. He described a non-alcoholic, sweet, milk-white boza predominantly made by Albanians. During this period, boza was a favored drink among the janissaries in the Ottoman army, valued for its warming and strengthening properties. While excessive consumption leading to intoxication was deemed sinful, moderate consumption was tolerated. By the 19th century, the sweet, non-alcoholic Albanian boza gained favor at the Ottoman palace, while the sour, alcoholic variant traditionally made by Armenians fell out of popularity. In 1876, the brothers Haci Ibrahim and Haci Sadik established a boza shop in the Vefa district of Istanbul. Their thick, tart boza became renowned throughout the city, and their shop, Vefa Bozacısı, remains operational today, managed by their descendants. It has become a minor tourist attraction. Other notable boza vendors in Turkey include Karakedi Bozacısı in Eskişehir, Akman Boza Salonu in Ankara, and Soydan in Pazarcık, Bilecik. In North Macedonia, the most famous boza shop is Apche, located in the Debar Maalo area of Skopje. Founded in 1934 by Isman Kadri, nicknamed Apche (meaning the pill) for the drink's reputed health benefits, the shop was renamed in 1940. Other well-known boza establishments in Skopje include Palma and Sheherezada. The tradition of boza-making is shared by both ethnic Albanians and Macedonians, as reflected in cultural works such as the 1928 play Lenche Kumanovce/Begalka by Vasil Iljoski, which features a boza vendor character. Boza production varies across Turkic regions, with different cereals used as the base ingredient. In Kyrgyzstan, it is made with crushed wheat; in Crimea, with wheat flour; and in Turkmenistan, with coarsely ground rice meal. In Albania, maize and a small amount of grain flour are used. The Vefa Boza recipe involves boiling hulled millet in water, cooling the mixture, sieving it, and adding water and sugar. A scientific study conducted by the Turkish Science and Technology Institute for Vefa Bozacısı found boza to be highly nutritious, containing 1,000 calories per liter, multiple vitamins (A, B, and E), and lactic acid, which aids digestion. Due to its perishable nature, boza was traditionally not sold during summer months in Turkey, with vendors offering alternative beverages like grape juice or lemonade. However, modern refrigeration has made year-round availability possible. In Albania and North Macedonia, boza is produced and consumed as a refreshing beverage throughout the year. There is a controversial claim that boza can enhance breast size in women. It is also recommended for lactating mothers, as it is believed to stimulate milk production.
